title: What a Computer Is
summary: A computer is a machine that follows a list of instructions, very fast and without getting bored. Every computer, from the first one to your phone, has the same four parts - input, processing, memory and output - and all of them are built from switches that are either on or off.
markdown:
## A machine that follows instructions A calculator can add. A computer can add too, but that is not what makes it a computer. What makes it a computer is that it follows a **list of instructions** - a **program** - and the list can be changed. Give a computer a list that says "add up these marks and work out the average", and it is a school report tool. Give it a different list and the very same machine plays music, draws a game or sends a message. Nothing inside it changes except the list. > [!abstract] In one sentence > A computer is a machine that stores a list of instructions and carries them out one after another, very fast, and can store and change the information it is working on. Each instruction is tiny: "add these two numbers", "copy this number over there", "if this number is zero, jump to that instruction". A computer is not clever. It is **fast** - billions of tiny steps a second - and **exact**: it never skips a step and never gets bored. Everything impressive a computer does is built out of a huge number of simple steps. ## The four parts Every computer ever built has the same four jobs, done by different parts: ```mermaid flowchart LR I["Input
keyboard, mouse,
touch screen, microphone"] --> P["Processing
the CPU follows
the instructions"] P <--> M["Memory
holds the program
and its data"] P --> O["Output
screen, speaker,
printer"] ``` | Part | Job | Examples | |---|---|---| | **Input** | Gets information into the computer | Keyboard, mouse, touch screen, camera, microphone, network | | **Processing** | Carries out the instructions | The CPU (central processing unit), the GPU for graphics | | **Memory** | Holds the program and the data it is working on | RAM while running, an SSD or hard drive to keep things when the power is off | | **Output** | Gets results out | Screen, speakers, printer, network | Your phone has all four: the touch screen is both input and output, the chip inside does the processing, and it has memory for the apps that are running and storage for your photos. ## Hardware and software - **Hardware** is the part you can touch: chips, wires, the screen. - **Software** is the instructions: the programs. You cannot touch a program; it is information, like the words of a recipe are different from the paper they are printed on. The same hardware runs different software. That is the whole trick, and it is why a computer is so much more useful than a machine built for one job. ## Everything is switches Deep down, a computer is made of **switches**. Not light switches you flip by hand, but microscopic electronic ones called **transistors**, which can be turned on and off by electricity - billions of times a second. A modern chip has billions of them. A switch has only two states: **on** or **off**. Write on as `1` and off as `0`, and you have a **bit** (short for *binary digit*). Every number, letter, photo and program inside a computer is stored as patterns of bits. This course spends a whole milestone on that, because it is the foundation everything else stands on. ```demo-bits title: Eight switches bits: 8 value: 77 ``` Click the switches above. Eight of them together hold one number from 0 to 255. You will learn exactly why in milestone 2. ## Layers A computer is built in **layers**, each one hiding the details of the one below: | Layer | What it deals in | Course milestone | |---|---|---| | Apps you use | Buttons, pictures, words | | | Programming languages | `print("Hello")` | 5 | | Operating system | Files, windows, running programs | 6 | | Machine code | Instructions as numbers | 4 | | Logic gates and the CPU | AND, OR, adding bits | 4 | | Bits | 0 and 1 | 2, 3 | | Transistors | Switches made of silicon | 1, 4 | Programmers mostly work in the top layers, but knowing what is underneath explains why computers behave the way they do: why a number can "overflow", why `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`, why a program can crash. By the end of this course you will be able to follow a single line of code all the way down to the switches. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What makes a computer different from a calculator? - It can work with much bigger numbers + It follows a stored program that can be changed - It has a screen and a keyboard > A calculator is built for one job. A computer runs whatever list of instructions it is given, so one machine can do many different jobs. ? Which part of a computer carries out the instructions? - The memory + The CPU - The keyboard > The CPU (central processing unit) does the processing. Memory holds the program and data it works on. ? What is a bit? - A small program + A single 0 or 1 - Eight numbers in a row > "Bit" is short for binary digit: one switch that is off or on. Everything inside a computer is stored as patterns of bits. ```

cards.q: What makes a computer different from a calculator?
cards.a:
It follows a stored program that can be changed

A calculator is built for one job. A computer runs whatever list of instructions it is given, so one machine can do many different jobs.
